q: Match the proteinuria test with the threshold that makes it positive — 1) 24-hour urinary protein 2) Urine protein:creatinine ratio 3) Urine dipstick used for OPD screening … A) At least 300 mg per 24 hours B) At least 0.3 C) At least +1
exp: Proteinuria is 300 mg or more in 24 hours, a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 0.3 or more, and a dipstick of +1 or more for OPD screening; 24-hour urinary protein is the gold standard.

q: Match the severe-feature test with its end-organ-damage threshold — 1) Platelet count 2) Serum creatinine 3) Hepatic transaminases … A) Below 1 lakh/mm³ B) At least 1.1 mg/dL C) At least twice the normal level
exp: Severe features are a platelet count below 1 lakh/mm³, serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL or more, and transaminases at least twice normal.

q: All of the following are listed as NON-differentiating between mild and severe pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: A blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher
The degree of proteinuria
Oliguria
Intrauterine growth restriction
exp: The degree of proteinuria, oliguria and IUGR are all listed as non-differentiating; a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg or higher does differentiate mild from severe pre-eclampsia.

q: All of the following are listed visual warning symptoms of impending eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Presbyopia alone, corrected by reading glasses
Diplopia
Blurring of vision
Scotoma or blindness
exp: The source lists diplopia, blurred vision, scotoma and blindness as warning symptoms of impending eclampsia; presbyopia alone is not one of them.

q: A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks has a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg with 2+ urine protein. Her platelets, creatinine and transaminases are normal and she has no headache or visual symptoms. How is this classified?
opts: Mild pre-eclampsia, the pressure being 140/90 to under 160/110
Severe pre-eclampsia on the degree of proteinuria alone
Gestational hypertension, since no end-organ damage is present
Chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia
exp: Mild pre-eclampsia is a blood pressure of 140/90 to under 160/110 mmHg without severe features; the degree of proteinuria does not differentiate mild from severe.

q: A woman with pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks reports a severe headache that has not responded to her usual analgesics, and her blood pressure is now 160/110 mmHg. Which feature is she showing?
opts: Impending eclampsia, from a severe headache unrelieved by usual medication
Migraine with aura, occurring independently of her pre-eclampsia
Cerebral venous thrombosis, needing immediate cranial imaging
The physiological headache of pregnancy, needing only reassurance
exp: Impending eclampsia includes a severe headache not relieved by usual medication, alongside visual symptoms and epigastric pain.

q: A 36-year-old with known chronic hypertension, previously well controlled on methyldopa, is now 28 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure has become uncontrollable and she has developed new 2+ proteinuria. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia
Gestational hypertension alone, since she was hypertensive before
Transient hypertension of pregnancy, needing no treatment
Mild pre-eclampsia, which carries the best prognosis
exp: Superimposed pre-eclampsia is chronic hypertension with uncontrollable blood pressure, new proteinuria or end-organ damage after 20 weeks, and it carries a bad prognosis.

q: A 26-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure before the onset of labour pain. Which type of eclampsia is this, and what is its prognosis?
opts: Antepartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Intrapartum eclampsia, the commonest type and the worst prognosis
Postpartum eclampsia, which is uncommon and has the best prognosis
Atypical eclampsia, needing anticonvulsants for six months
exp: Antepartum eclampsia is the most common type and has the worst prognosis; postpartum eclampsia is within 48 hours of delivery and onset beyond 48 hours is atypical.

q: Which statement about edema in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: Edema is pathological when it does not subside with rest and involves non-dependent parts
Edema is pathological only when it is confined to the ankles after standing
Any edema appearing in pregnancy is by definition a severe feature
Edema is always absent in pregnancy-induced hypertension
exp: Pathological edema does not improve with rest and is present in dependent and non-dependent parts, unlike physiological dependent edema which settles overnight.

q: Which statement about the investigations emphasised in all pre-eclampsia patients is TRUE?
opts: Liver function tests, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three highlighted tests
Karyotyping, TORCH serology and VDRL are the three highlighted tests
Serum bile acids, indirect Coombs test and OGTT are the three highlighted tests
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, calcium and HbA1c are the three highlighted tests
exp: LFT, serum creatinine and platelet count are the three investigations highlighted for every pre-eclampsia patient.

q: Which statement about the postpartum course of pregnancy-induced hypertension is TRUE?
opts: Blood pressure usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery
Blood pressure usually normalises within 48 hours of delivery
Hypertension persisting beyond 12 weeks is still called gestational hypertension
Blood pressure never returns to normal after pregnancy-induced hypertension
exp: PIH usually normalises within 12 weeks of delivery; a blood pressure still raised at 12 weeks postpartum is reclassified as chronic hypertension.

q: Fill up: Epigastric pain in impending eclampsia is attributed to a ______ that is stretching the ______.
opts: Subcapsular hematoma; liver capsule
Subcapsular hematoma; splenic capsule
Retroplacental clot; uterine serosa
Subcapsular hematoma; renal capsule
exp: Epigastric pain reflects subcapsular hematoma and stretching of the liver capsule.

q: Fill up: The notes state that all women with pre-eclampsia should be ______.
opts: Admitted
Observed at home without any tests
Managed on an OPD basis only
Discharged after a single blood-pressure reading
exp: The notes state that all pre-eclampsia patients should be admitted.

q: Match the day of the medical-abortion protocol with what it involves — 1) Day 1 2) Day 3 3) Day 15 … A) Misoprostol 800 micrograms B) Mifepristone 200 mg as a single oral tablet C) Follow-up to confirm completion
exp: Day 1 is a single 200-mg oral mifepristone tablet, day 3 is misoprostol 800 micrograms (vaginal, then sublingual, then oral), and day 15 is follow-up to ensure complete abortion.

q: Fill up: First-trimester medical abortion is stated to be used up to ______ weeks, that is ______ days.
exp: First-trimester medical abortion is used up to 9 weeks, or 63 days.

q: Fill up: Listed routes for misoprostol are ______, sublingual, per-vaginal and per-rectal.
opts: Oral
Intravenous
Intra-amniotic
Intramuscular
exp: Misoprostol may be given orally, sublingually, per vaginam or per rectum.

q: Which statement about ultrasound in medical termination of pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Ultrasound is not routinely required in MTP
Ultrasound is mandatory in every case before MTP
Ultrasound is used only to calculate the anti-D dose
Ultrasound is required at every follow-up visit after MTP
exp: USG is not routinely required in MTP, but is indicated for uncertain LMP, a size not matching the period of gestation, abdominal pain, or continuous spotting with an open os on day 15.

q: Which statement about hysterotomy is TRUE?
opts: Hysterotomy means opening the uterus to remove the products of conception
Hysterotomy is the procedure used to close the cervix with a cerclage stitch
Hysterotomy is a test performed to detect fetal anemia
Hysterotomy is a recognised variety of ectopic pregnancy
exp: Hysterotomy means opening the uterus to take out products of conception.

q: All of the following are listed contraindications to medical abortion EXCEPT:
opts: Rh-negative blood group on its own
Hemoglobin below 8 g/dL
Uncontrolled hypertension at or above 160/100 mmHg
Chronic adrenal failure
exp: Listed contraindications include hemoglobin below 8 g/dL, uncontrolled hypertension of 160/100 mmHg or more, uncontrolled seizures, chronic adrenal failure and inability to comply with follow-up; Rh negativity alone is not one.

q: A 24-year-old woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea requests medical termination. She has no contraindications and is able to return for review. Which first-trimester regimen is listed?
opts: Mifepristone followed by misoprostol
Methotrexate followed by folinic acid
Magnesium sulfate with nifedipine
Insulin with metformin
exp: First-trimester medical abortion uses mifepristone plus misoprostol, and is managed on an OPD basis.

q: Match each cause of antepartum haemorrhage with when or how often it occurs — 1) Commonest cause 2) Second commonest cause 3) Bleeding commonest at the time of labour … A) Abruptio placenta B) Placenta previa C) Uterine rupture
exp: Abruptio placenta is the commonest cause of APH, placenta previa the second commonest, and uterine rupture is commonest at the time of labour.

q: Match the definition to the condition — 1) Placenta lying in the lower uterine segment 2) Premature separation of a normally located placenta 3) Fetal blood escaping through the mother's vagina … A) Abruptio placenta B) Placenta previa C) Vasa previa
exp: Placenta previa is a placenta in the lower uterine segment; abruptio is premature separation of a normally located placenta; vasa previa means fetal blood loss coming out through the mother's vagina.

q: All of the following count as antepartum haemorrhage EXCEPT:
opts: A blood-stained mucus show in preterm labour
Bleeding from placental abruption with a tender, contracting uterus
Painless recurrent bleeding from placenta previa in the third trimester
Bleeding from vasa previa accompanied by fetal bradycardia
exp: A show is mucus with a little blood from the cervix; antepartum haemorrhage means bleeding from the placental site or vessels, so a preterm show is not APH.

q: Fill up: For the diagnosis of placenta previa, the placenta must lie within ______ of the internal os.
opts: 2 cm
5 cm
10 cm
1 cm
exp: Placenta previa is defined by a placenta-to-internal-os distance of 2 cm or less.

q: Which statement about bleeding in placenta previa is TRUE?
opts: The placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released
The placenta separates centrally, releasing thromboplastin
Fetal distress is the earliest and most constant feature
The bleeding is consistently painful and dark red
exp: In placenta previa the shearing force opens venous sinuses of the intervillous space; the placenta does not separate and no thromboplastin is released.

q: Which statement about thromboplastin release in abruptio placenta is TRUE?
opts: It produces a tense tender uterus, labour, tissue necrosis and DIC
It produces uterine relaxation with painless bleeding
It limits bleeding by promoting local clot formation at the site
It has no systemic effect and stays within the uterine cavity
exp: Thromboplastin causes a tense, tender, rigid uterus, initiates labour, raises matrix metalloproteinase with tissue necrosis and blood loss, and can progress to DIC.

q: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks presents with painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding and the placenta has not yet been located on scan. Which examination is contraindicated until placenta previa is ruled out?
opts: Per vaginal examination, until placenta previa has been excluded
Per abdominal examination of the fundal height and lie
Recording of the maternal pulse and blood pressure
Speculum inspection performed after the ultrasound
exp: Per vaginal examination is contraindicated in third-trimester APH until placenta previa is excluded.

q: A low-lying placenta is noted on the 20-week anomaly scan of an asymptomatic woman. Why is placenta previa not diagnosed at this stage?
opts: Placental migration occurs with differential growth of the lower segment in the third trimester
Ultrasound is unsafe before the third trimester of pregnancy
Bleeding from placenta previa never occurs before the third trimester
The internal os does not begin to dilate until the third trimester
exp: Differential growth of the lower uterine segment in the third trimester migrates the placenta upwards, so the diagnosis is reserved for the third trimester.

q: A woman at 38 weeks has painless vaginal bleeding with fetal bradycardia, and the blood lost is fetal blood coming out through the mother's vagina. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Vasa previa, with fetal blood escaping through the mother's vagina
Abruptio placenta, with premature separation of the placenta
Placenta previa, with the placenta in the lower uterine segment
Uterine rupture, with bleeding from the previous scar site
exp: Vasa previa means fetal blood loss coming out through the mother's vagina, which is why it presents with fetal bradycardia.
The best time for ultrasound assessment of placenta previa is 32 weeks and 36 weeks, the third-trimester window in which the diagnosis is made.

q: Fill up: Primary PPH occurs within ______ of delivery, and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to ______ afterwards.
opts: 24 hours; 12 weeks
6 hours; 24 hours
1 hour; 7 days
48 hours; 6 weeks
exp: Primary PPH is within 24 hours of birth and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum.

q: All of the following are specific risk factors for TRAUMATIC PPH EXCEPT:
opts: Anaemia in the mother before delivery
Instrumental delivery
Breech extraction
Obstructed labour with tachysystole
exp: Traumatic PPH follows tears and lacerations from operative delivery, malpresentation, obstructed or very fast labour and high parity; anaemia is a maternal rather than a traumatic risk factor.

q: Which statement about intrapartum risk factors for PPH is TRUE?
opts: Prolonged or precipitate labour, induction, instrumental delivery and general anaesthesia all raise the risk
Epidural analgesia and active management of the third stage raise the risk
Ambulation, continuous support and the left lateral position raise the risk
Oral fluids in labour and intermittent auscultation are intrapartum risk factors
exp: Intrapartum risk factors exhaust or damage the uterus and birth canal; the measures in the other options are neutral or protective.

q: A woman undergoes postpartum dilatation and curettage for retained products of conception. What is she at the highest risk of, and what best prevents PPH in the first place?
opts: Asherman syndrome; active management of the third stage of labour
Uterine inversion; an oxytocin bolus given with the anterior shoulder
Placenta accreta spectrum; routine misoprostol in the third stage
Endometritis; early clamping of the umbilical cord
exp: Postpartum D&C carries the highest risk of Asherman syndrome; the best method of preventing PPH is active management of the third stage of labour.
